To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
amphetamine increases activation of brain regions associated with the processing of auditory and motor information.

amphetamine increases brain activation during auditory and motor tasks in the primary sensory areas and in areas that have been implicated in the attentional mechanisms that modulate sensory processing.

the drug increased the number of voxels that showed increased activity during the performance of two tasks, a tone discrimination task (auditory task) and a right-hand finger-tapping task (motor task).

understanding how drugs of abuse affect brain function and behavior.
the study of the neural mechanisms of attention, learning, memory and decision making in humans.
the study of the effects of psychostimulants on the brain, with the ultimate goal of understanding the mechanisms of action of these drugs in normal and pathological conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
amphetamine increased the number of brain areas activated by two different tasks.
d-amphetamine increases brain activation during auditory and motor tasks, and this increase may reflect a direct drug effect on neuronal activity.
the results are consistent with a direct effect of d-amphetamine on the activity of the primary auditory cortices and the primary sensorimotor cortices.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
amphetamine increases brain activity in the primary auditory and primary motor cortices.
amphetamine increased the number of voxels showing activation during the performance of a simple motor task or a tone discrimination task.
d-amphetamine increased the number of voxels in primary auditory and sensorimotor cortices activated by auditory and motor tasks, respectively, and did not affect the magnitude of activation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is very sensitive to the effects of stimulant drugs, and that these effects are very specific to the task being performed.

amphetamine can be used to enhance the BOLD signal in the brain and that this enhancement can be used to increase the signal to noise ratio of the fMRI experiment and thus increase the sensitivity of the technique.
